slides.title: Why frequentist statistics matters for ML
slides.body:
Most ML teams reach for statistics when they need to defend a number. 'Is this 1% accuracy improvement real?' 'Is this customer-engagement lift significant?' 'How precise is this confidence interval?' These are statistical questions with statistical answers.

**Frequentist statistics** treats parameters as fixed unknown quantities and data as random. The core conceptual move: imagine running the same experiment many times; what's the distribution of statistics you'd compute?

Key constructs:
- **Sampling distribution**: the distribution of a statistic across hypothetical repeated experiments.
- **Standard error**: the standard deviation of a sampling distribution.
- **Confidence interval**: an interval that, in repeated experiments, would contain the true parameter X% of the time.

Frequentist statistics is the dominant flavor in industry ML evaluation. Every reported 'p < 0.05' is a frequentist statement. Understanding the foundations is non-negotiable for anyone who designs experiments or interprets ML evaluation results.

slides.title: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
slides.body:
**MLE**: given a parameterized statistical model `p(x | θ)` and observed data `x_1, ..., x_n`, find the `θ` that maximizes the likelihood:

$$\hat{\theta}_{MLE} = \arg\max_\theta \prod_i p(x_i | \theta) = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log p(x_i | \theta)$$

The second form (log-likelihood) is what you actually optimize — sum is more numerically stable than product.

**Why MLE is everywhere in ML**:
- **Cross-entropy loss** is the negative log-likelihood for classification under a categorical model.
- **MSE** is the negative log-likelihood for regression under a Gaussian-noise model.
- **Logistic regression** maximizes log-likelihood under Bernoulli observations.
- **Language model training**: maximize log-likelihood of the next token given context.

ML's loss functions are MLE in disguise. Understanding the statistical framing helps you read papers + design new objectives.

**Properties**:
- **Consistent**: as `n → ∞`, `Ŝ_MLE → θ_true` (under regularity conditions).
- **Asymptotically normal**: `√n (Ŝ_MLE - θ) → N(0, I^{-1}(θ))` where `I` is the Fisher information.
- **Asymptotically efficient**: achieves the Cramer-Rao lower bound on variance.

These are theoretical guarantees about large-sample behavior. Small-sample performance can deviate; MLE on tiny datasets is biased + high-variance.

slides.title: The bootstrap
slides.body:
How do you estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic when you don't know the underlying distribution? **Resample your data with replacement.**

**Bootstrap procedure**:

```
original_data = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_n)

for b in range(B):                    # B = 1000+ typical
    bootstrap_sample = sample(original_data, n, replace=True)
    statistic_b = compute(bootstrap_sample)

bootstrap_distribution = (statistic_1, statistic_2, ..., statistic_B)
```

The distribution of bootstrap statistics approximates the sampling distribution of the original statistic.

**What you can compute**:
- **Standard error**: `std(bootstrap_distribution)`.
- **Confidence interval**: `(2.5th percentile, 97.5th percentile)` for a 95% CI.
- **Bias**: `mean(bootstrap_distribution) - statistic(original)`.

**Why this is magical**: no parametric assumptions. No 'assume the data is Gaussian'. Works for any well-behaved statistic — the median, the IQR, ratios, regression coefficients.

In ML evaluation: **always bootstrap your benchmark scores**. Reporting 'accuracy = 0.873' without an interval is statistically meaningless. Reporting 'accuracy = 0.873 ± 0.011 (95% CI)' is honest.

When bootstrap fails: very small samples (~n < 30), heavy-tailed distributions where the variance doesn't exist. Edge cases; not common in ML evaluation.

question.question: Why is reporting an ML benchmark accuracy without a confidence interval statistically meaningless?
options: Accuracy is a sample statistic; its true value depends on which test set was sampled. Without an interval (or standard error), you can't tell whether two reported accuracies — say, 0.873 vs 0.881 — are statistically different or noise. The interval is the difference between 'we beat the baseline' and 'maybe we did, maybe we didn't'
Reviewers always reject papers without intervals
question.explanation: Sample statistics have sampling distributions. The point estimate is the most likely value; the interval tells you the uncertainty. Two methods reporting 0.873 vs 0.881 might be indistinguishable (overlapping 95% CIs) or genuinely different (disjoint CIs). Without intervals, you can't tell. Bootstrap is the universal solution; it costs ~1000× a single eval but is cheap compared to model training. Most ML papers underreport this; the field has been getting better.

slides.title: Sampling distributions in detail
slides.body:
The **sampling distribution** of a statistic is *the* core frequentist concept. Imagine running your experiment many times. Each experiment produces data `x_1, ..., x_n` and a statistic (e.g., the sample mean). The distribution of statistics across these hypothetical repetitions is the sampling distribution.

**Central Limit Theorem (CLT)**: for many statistics (sample means, regression coefficients), the sampling distribution is approximately Gaussian as `n → ∞`. Mean = the true parameter; std = standard error.

This is why so many statistical methods assume Gaussian errors: not because data is Gaussian, but because *sampling distributions* are. The CLT is the workhorse of frequentist inference.

**Standard error**: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. For the sample mean: `SE = σ / √n`. So:
- Bigger sample → smaller SE → more precise estimate.
- Bigger underlying variance → bigger SE.

**Confidence intervals**: under CLT, `(estimate ± 1.96 · SE)` covers the true parameter ~95% of the time across hypothetical repeats. Note: the interval 'covers the parameter'; the parameter doesn't 'fall in the interval' — common confusion.

For ML benchmarks: the SE on accuracy `p` is `√(p(1-p)/n)`. For a 1000-example test set with `p = 0.85`: `SE ≈ 0.011`. So accuracies of 0.847 and 0.853 are likely within sampling noise.

Bootstrap is more general than CLT-based formulas — works for any statistic, not just means. But CLT-based formulas are cheap closed forms that work for the common cases.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Frequentist foundations are the substrate. Next: hypothesis testing — the formal machinery for deciding 'is this difference real or noise?'.

Next: [[hypothesis-testing]] — null hypotheses, p-values, multiple testing.

Key takeaways:
- Sampling distribution: distribution of a statistic across hypothetical repeated experiments
- MLE: maximize log-likelihood; underlies cross-entropy, MSE, logistic regression
- Bootstrap: resample with replacement; estimate sampling distribution non-parametrically
- CLT: sampling distribution is Gaussian for large n; SE = `σ/√n` for the mean
- ML benchmarks need confidence intervals; point estimates alone are statistically meaningless
